title: Great Teachers = Great Rememberers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens with a confession about forgetting former students' names, using it as a gateway to argue that the more consequential form of teacher memory concerns purpose, not people. The article draws on the learning principle that we remember what we think about to explain both why names fade and why first-principles thinking must be actively maintained. Stuart identifies four foundational questions — what is school for, what is my discipline for, why are these things good, and what are the best means of growing student mastery — as the core of what long-tenured, fire-sustaining teachers keep vividly in mind. He argues that vagueness in answering these questions correlates with burnout and ineffectiveness, while specificity and regular reflection correlate with long careers and lasting impact. The article functions as a quiet challenge to revisit foundational professional purpose.
points: The most professionally important form of teacher memory is not student names but foundational purposes — why school, this discipline, and education itself are good.
We remember what we think about; long-tenured teachers who sustain passion actively return to first-principles questions about education's purpose rather than letting answers go vague.
Four core questions mark the memory great teachers tend to keep sharp: what is school for, what is my subject for, why are these things good, and what are the best means of growing mastery.
Vague answers to foundational questions correlate with harder times in teaching; specific, worked-out, actively revisited answers correlate with long and impactful careers.

Cognitive overload from building mental models for 100+ students annually is real and explains why specific memories fade — but it makes purposeful remembering of first principles even more necessary.
quotes: I don't have the best memory in the world when it comes to the names of former students, and it really bothers me. I'll see a student I taught several years ago while doing some grocery shopping in our small town, and I'll recognize the face, remember the delight I took in teaching that student… but not their name.
We remember what we think about. This is why it's so important to teach our students to study via retrieval practice and get past the familiarity trap.

I can only think of so many things or people in a given day. In work like ours, there are a LOT of people to think about over the years. It's not a great feeling knowing the face but not the name of a former student, but it's just one of those limitations of the human mind that I've come to accept.

there are very important things that I think we teachers are prone to forgetting. I'm not talking about names here — I'm talking about purpose, about first principles, about the reasons that an education is good.

It's remembering these things that drives me to write and talk about teaching like I do. I've met enough 30+ year educators who sustain the fire to teach to recognize that one of their common traits is that they are exceptionally good at remembering the answers to a few basic questions

The vaguer your answers to these questions, the worse off you'll tend to be. The less you think about and work out the implications of the answers to these questions, the harder time you'll tend to have.
